title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
description: Cleveland Police's Chief Constable has said she is proud of her "brave" force but that it was being "let down" by the way it was funded, following a f
body: Cleveland Police's Chief Constable has said she is proud of her "brave" force but that it was being "let down" by the way it was funded, following a fatal crash which killed seven people including two police officers. In her first sit-down interview since the A66 crash, speaking exclusively to the BBC, Victoria Fuller said the force needed to become part of a larger force with greater resources.She said her officers are dealing with some of the highest crime levels in the country akin to those faced by metropolitan forces, but with less than half the number of officers.Multiple people have since been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash. A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news."No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra £2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra £20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.At the same time, Fuller said Cleveland Police had experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force."It absolutely needs to change," she said. Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues."We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fueling organised crime."When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said. "They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."The five who died in the Volkswagen on 22 August were aged between 17 and 23. Four of them had previous convictions, including for assaulting police officers and theft, Cleveland Police previously said.Since the crash, the force has responded to at least two incidents it believes are in retaliation for the crash.It has also had to grapple with a house fire in Middlesbrough that killed a woman and her niece, and left several others injured, which police could not rule out was linked to organised crime.A 23-year-old man has been charged with murder in relation to the deaths of Natalie McDonald, 34, and Valentina Foster, seven.Fuller also paid tribute to the two officers who died in the A66 crash - PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough."My heart goes out to their families - it really does," she said. "My grief can't compare to theirs, nor to the officers and staff who've worked closely with Matty and Tom for a long time."The Home Office said it was grateful to Cleveland Police for delivering a robust response in difficult circumstances. A spokesperson said: "We have been in regular contact with Cleveland Police and local leaders, ensuring they have the support they need and engaging on their financial concerns."This additional £2m targeted funding will help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime. Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026/2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash."We have also committed to a wider review of the police funding formula to ensure that force funding is fair and responsive to local needs."

schema.headline: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding

title: Nigel Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judiciary in Reform conference speech
description: Nigel Farage has insisted a Reform UK government would deliver where other parties have failed, as he set out his priorities in his annual conference
body: Nigel Farage has insisted a Reform UK government would deliver where other parties have failed, as he set out his priorities in his annual conference speech. He said Reform's pledges for its first 100 days in power would include stopping small boat crossings, cutting energy bills by £250 a year and ending the net zero "lunacy".To eliminate "obstacles" to his plans, Farage said he would declare a "national emergency" and threatened to overhaul the House of Lords and how judges are appointed if they stood in the way.In a speech interrupted several times by protesters, the Reform leader was also forced to address allegations over donations which emerged in an undercover investigation.Reform had been hoping to use its annual conference to regain momentum after a difficult summer dominated by questions over the party's finances.However, the main day of the conference was overshadowed after two senior party officials stepped down and Reform launched an investigation into claims about funding aired during a Channel 4 News report on Thursday evening, which was filmed by Verbatim Investigations, a group founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting.In the undercover filming, the two men suggested a way around electoral law to secure foreign donations for the party, one of which would have totalled £500,000.Farage insisted "the party has done nothing wrong" and "has taken no illegal money", claiming the allegations had been made "because they're scared of us".In his speech, which was light on new policy announcements, Farage said the country needed a government "that actually delivers on its promises" and "we're the only people capable of doing it".He argued the Tories "had 14 years in power and failed absolutely miserably", while Labour's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham "says he needs 10 years", a reference to the PM's promise to set out a 10-year plan for the country later this year.If Reform wins the next general election, Farage pledged to sack ministers who fail to deliver on their promises in their first 100 days in the job "and replace them with somebody else with the courage to do it".Setting out his plans to call a "national emergency" if Reform wins power, Farage said: "Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, for six days a week until we pass the necessary legislation."He said he expected the House of Lords to "honour" Reform's policy pledges but if they refused to do so threatened to appoint hundreds of new peers so the party had a majority in the upper chamber."And if that proves difficult, we will hold a referendum on the current composition of the House of Lords, and they would be swept away by a British public appalled by them," he added.Identifying the judiciary as another possible "obstacle", Farage promised to remove the ability of judges to rely on conventions like the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which critics blame for hindering some deportations."We don't want the courts striking down, do we, the will of the people," he said."Parliament makes the law, judges interpret the law. We will do whatever it takes, and perhaps have to consider how judicial appointments work in the future."Meanwhile, he said civil servants who "try to obstruct us" would be removed from their posts and replaced by people from the world of business. "I'm tired of being told what can't be done," the Reform leader said."That is not what the public want. The public want action, the public want genuine change, the public do not want any more of the same. And our attitude is can do, and will do."Predicting that Burnham would call an early general election in spring 2027, Farage attempted to use his speech to convince the public Reform was ready to govern.Stressing he now had a team of spokespeople with "frontline experience", he said the party was planning to broaden its expertise."There are more big jobs to fill, and I'm looking and working on defence, health, and the other areas," he added.In his speech, Farage also hailed a "historic agreement" on small boat returns, signed earlier between Reform and France's hard-right National Rally party.The deal sets out how a Reform government would intercept boats in the English Channel and return them to France using the Navy, with France "ordinarily" accepting those on board.It was signed by the National Rally President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of French presidential elections in April next year, after he gave a speech to the main conference hall.Farage took to the stage after a long delay, which he told delegates was due to a "security alert".He took the opportunity to walk through the crowd and greet delegates during the delay.His speech was also interrupted several times by protesters, including two women who held up a banner reading "Reform works for billionaires".They were booed by audience members who shouted "out", as they were removed by security.Farage laughed off the disruption, chanting "boring, boring, boring".Reform is no longer consistently topping national opinion polls, after more than a year of enjoying a comfortable lead.Meanwhile, Labour's ratings have risen since Burnham entered Downing Street, and Reform has lost some support to Restore Britain, the new right-wing party founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

schema.headline: Nigel Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judiciary in Reform conference speech

title: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims
description: More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Br
body: More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.However in a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.When asked about if the prime minister believed the UK had the necessary forces to defend the sovereignty of the islands the spokesperson said "they will remain so far as long as the islanders wish"."Our armed forces are on standby 24/7 to protect the UK and our interests", the spokesperson added.Announcing his plan for sanctions in a national address on Thursday, Milei reiterated that the Falkland Islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.He said: "There can be no argument. They are part of the Argentine territory."The islanders on their usurped territory do not have a legitimate right to self-determination and any argument on any such self-determination is invalid."Milei described the Sea Lion oilfield as a "clear and present danger", and said if Argentina does not act swiftly, "they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before."He continued: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward".It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government." The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.  The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas."That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders." Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable"."Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands. "We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said. Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies". "If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others." Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

schema.headline: Falkland Islands: UK support 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims

title: A66 crash: Distrust and fear hang over Middlesbrough
description: It is just after 8pm in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, and the light is fading.Two teenagers in balaclavas tear across a park on a muddy red quad bik
body: It is just after 8pm in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, and the light is fading.Two teenagers in balaclavas tear across a park on a muddy red quad bike, pulling wheelies as they pass a man walking his dog.Younger boys, some not yet in their teens, gather excitedly around the bike.We're here because Grangetown and neighbouring South Bank now find themselves at the centre of a large police operation, with fears organised crime is out of control after the deaths of two police officers and five young men in a car crash on the A66.Suddenly one of our team is hit by a pellet, which appears to have been fired from the group. It stings but he's OK.Then the quad riders pull over for a chat, engine running.I ask the riders if it is normal to be driving around the park on a quad bike."Yeah, this isn't any special day," the passenger says. "You're born and bred and brought up with it. What do you expect? You don't know anything different."Since the crash, more than 20 people have been arrested in Middlesbrough and the surrounding area as part of a wider operation into what police have called "serious and organised crime".Sources say there are two feuding gangs at the centre of a spike in violence.Is this area out of control, I ask the quad bike riders. "No. Definitely not."Then they reveal something we repeatedly heard from young people here. They do not trust the police."They're saying there are gangs, but there are no gangs," the driver says. "It's not London, mate. Do you know what I mean?"Like many young people here, they blame the police for the deaths on the A66. The circumstances remain under independent investigation.What we do know is that on Saturday 22 August, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way along the A66 and collided head-on with a police vehicle.PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed. So were all five people in the Passat: Michael Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae and Cole Worthy, both 17.Four of the five young men killed had amassed 30 convictions between them for offences including car theft, drug possession, assaulting police officers and driving offences. Cahill had no convictions.The chain of events that ended on the A66 is believed to have begun eight miles away, in a quiet suburban street in Acklam.It feels a world away from Grangetown. Hanging baskets and neat front gardens line the bay windows of 1930s semi-detached homes.Many residents are reluctant to speak. Why? Because of what happened to one house here that stands behind large metal barriers.A car was rammed into the bay window, exposing the room inside. Some of the other windows were also smashed.Fragments of lights and bumper remain scattered across the driveway.The home belongs to Cole Worthy's father, Gye Worthy, and the ramming happened on the same night Cole died.Police say the car used in the attack was a Volvo XC60. The BBC understands that Cole Worthy and the four others then set off in the Passat to find the Volvo.Now neighbours describe a street living in fear and say the home has been targeted for more than a year.There is no suggestion that Gye Worthy is involved in criminal activity.All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one."Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town."This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown."It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"He blames drugs."It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife."No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying"."Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.As darkness settles over Grangetown, the quad bike is still circling the field and one woman, who moved here not long ago, asks us to move our car from outside her home, frightened we will be targeted and her property will become collateral damage.But what worries her more is her children's future. "I'm terrified my son will end up like them, he's only 10, I don't want him to grow up like that," she says gesturing to the lads with balaclavas tearing up the grass on the quad bike.Additional reporting by Brijesh Patel.

schema.headline: A66 crash: Distrust and fear hang over Middlesbrough

title: Women's Super League: How London City Lionesses proved they can live up to the hype
description: There was an expectation on London City Lionesses to live up to the hype and deliver in the Women's Super League's season opener - and they did.Eder M
body: There was an expectation on London City Lionesses to live up to the hype and deliver in the Women's Super League's season opener - and they did.Eder Maestre's side showed they are not just a starting XI of superstars but a team who may gel quicker than many expected.They came away from Hayes Lane, in front of a full crowd of 5,402 home fans, with an impressive 2-1 victory over Manchester United. The scoreline could have been worse for United as London City dominated the first half and showed flashes of individual brilliance, amid a clear structure and intent.Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas made her debut and was the glue in midfield while others stole the limelight.US billionaire owner Michele Kang was also present, donning a new match shirt with her name on the back and posing for photos with fans before kick-off."It was really fun to win today," said Delphine Cascarino, one of many international stars in the London City squad. "I think we have a chance to do something this season. We are trying to build something huge and achieve big things and I think we have a chance."The tone was set in the first minute by London City, immediately showing their intent with a strike from Alanna Kennedy in the first minute that won a corner.They allowed United no time to settle, pressing from the front and taking advantage of the visitors' hesitancy in possession.A flick from Putellas here and there, tenacity from Kennedy and quick feet from Grace Geyoro were all frequently on show.But it was the fluidity of London City's link-up play that caught the eye - a group of superstars looking like a good team in the first game of the season. Surely it pleased manager Maestre?"Yeah, I think we were really strong, mostly in the first half," said Maestre."We are facing Manchester United. You can't imagine you will be dominant for the whole game because they have a lot of good players. "The team showed how capable we are and what we were trying to create so I'm very proud."London City were a bit of an unknown entity in pre-season given the arrival of several big-name players.Ex-United and England goalkeeper Mary Earps started on the bench alongside fellow new arrival Nicole Anyomi but Spain's Mapi Leon and forward Rosa Kafaji started.Danielle van de Donk, who spent most of last season injured, starred and scored, while Kennedy's header brought the opener when it deflected off Julia Zigiotti.Putting the pieces together is the challenge with which Maestre has been tasked but Friday night was a fine start."It's one of the most challenging situations for coaches when you have many talented players but you are trying to align everyone on the same page and achieve something big," said Maestre. "We need very good positional game and that flexibility to feel strong in a match. That is why I'm really happy with the performance. "To have all the players on the same page and establish that relationship is really good."In contrast, opponents Manchester United - one of those London City hope to overtake this season - clearly need more time to adapt to new manager Eva Olid's ways.When she addressed the media for the first time on Thursday, the Spaniard promised brave, attacking football and a desire to dominate possession.But what transpired in a painful opening 45 minutes for United supporters was a team short on confidence and lacking threat, failing to produce a shot of any kind.The second half saw improvement but it came too late.Indeed, United did not have a shot on target until the ninth minute of second-half stoppage time, substitute Simi Awujo's goal giving the scoreline a friendlier look."I always say it's a process. In three weeks, I don't think we can believe we are a team that will dominate the ball and attack," said ex-Hearts boss Olid, who was appointed on 5 August."Of course, I think it's more something mental. In the first half,  I didn't feel like the players were believing. At half time I said: 'Listen, this is not us.'"In the first half, we were forcing things, the basics in possession were wrong and we were giving them the ball to attack. That is not what we want to be."In the second half, we were building through the middle, playing in the pockets and moving through the lines. That is us. That felt like my team in the second half."Olid said it was her job to help her players believe they can be better and was defiant when asked if United could compete with the quality displayed by London City.She said the difference between the two teams on the day was down to confidence."If we play as we did in the second half, I don't think the gap is that big," she added."I think the structure was wrong in attack - when the structure isn't right, the players are lost. We fixed that but mentally, the players were not believing. "London City pressed well and took our mistakes to create chances. They did very well in the first half but in the second half, I felt we were in the match."

schema.headline: Women's Super League: How London City Lionesses proved they can live up to the hype

title: Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem
description: Almost 100% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and it produces so much it earns nearly $200m (£147m) each year exporting hydroelectricity t
body: Almost 100% of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, and it produces so much it earns nearly $200m (£147m) each year exporting hydroelectricity to India and Bangladesh.But the very glaciers and mountains giving Nepal this massive natural advantage are succumbing to global warming - and last Wednesday's deadly floods have laid bare the risks to the nation's hydropower ambitions.More than 1,300 people were killed, while thousands more are still missing.The floods, which destroyed entire villages near the border of Nepal and Tibet, severely damaged 12 hydropower plants in the Trishuli River basin and knocked out more than 10% of Nepal's total power generation capacity. Operators tell the BBC they don't yet know if any of these facilities can be brought back to operation.The state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority, which owns six of the 12 damaged facilities, has assured Nepalese households that supply remains adequate. But its spokesman Rajan Dhakal acknowledges that with climate-related disasters becoming more frequent, "the time has come for a rethink of our hydropower policy".Only two-thirds of people in Nepal had access to electricity in 2010, and even connected households would face power cuts for up to 16 hours a day.An expansion of hydropower infrastructure alongside efforts to tackle corruption and boost energy imports from India to fill seasonal gaps meant that by 2018, most of Nepal was enjoying 24 hours of power supply per day.At present, there are 225 hydropower plants across Nepal with more than 3,900MW of installed capacity, according to the Nepal Electricity Authority - capable of powering some three million households simultaneously.Hundreds more such facilities are either being constructed or in the pipeline. Most of them are built high up in the mountains, where they can seize fast-flowing currents to generate power. These projects require little to no storage system.However, with the high-altitude regions of the Himalayas warming 50% faster than the global average, they face greater environmental risks. Preliminary investigations have pointed to a collapsed glacier and its bedrock as the cause of last week's flash flood.While scientists say it is too soon to draw any firm links to climate change, Nepal's Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority previously said more than nine in 10 disaster events recorded between 2018 and 2024 were "related to climate".Nepal's former Energy Minister Kulman Ghising, who called the catastrophic deluge a "once-in-a-century" event, says it holds lessons for designing plants and picking sites where they are built."We need to design the plants [to be more] resilient to the floods and, most importantly, adopt early-warning systems as well as robust emergency evacuation measures," he told environmental news outlet Mongabay.Potentially hundreds of hydropower labourers, engineers and residents are thought to be trapped inside the mud-filled tunnels of these plants since the floods hit.A "rethink" of Nepal's hydropower strategy could involve reservoir-based plants that need not be situated up in the mountains, says Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority. These could allow water to be stored and released as needed, but would also involve significant economic and environmental costs.Some question if Nepal has been too reliant on hydropower."We should not be putting all our eggs in one basket in these dangerous times," says renewable energy expert Kushal Gurung, who founded the clean tech firm WindPower Nepal."We need to seriously embrace other alternatives as well, like solar and wind. And for that we will need to revise our energy policy that is at the moment very pro-hydropower," he says.The claim is echoed by Vivek Shastry, researcher at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who argues that "meaningful additions of wind and solar generation is a resilience strategy that can limit single-point or interconnected electricity system failures in the future".A report from the German aid agency suggests the technical potential for energy production from solar power in Nepal is around 10 times larger, external than that of hydropower.  Puspa Sharma, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore's Institute of South Asian Studies, agrees Nepal has to diversify its energy sources, but warns this can be done "only to a limited extent"."While there is untapped capacity in wind and solar, hydropower really is the one that gives Nepal massive competitive advantage vis-a-vis its South Asian neighbours," he says, citing various studies comparing renewable energy potential in the region.Hydropower continues to dominate large-scale investments in Nepal, and some climate activists say the funding has continued despite known disaster risks.The Upper Trishuli-1 project, which has been all but destroyed after last week's floods, was one of Nepal's largest foreign direct investment ventures, valued at about $647m. Its backers include the Asian Development Bank and the International Finance Corporation.The Upper Trishuli 3A, which has also been severely hit, was funded by China's Export-Import Bank.Himanshu Thakkar, coordinator of the South Asia Network on Dams, Rivers & People, says international lenders were "acutely aware of the extreme danger to which they were exposing thousands of labourers, officials, residents, rivers, infrastructure and landscape"."Their own reports repeatedly highlighted it. But they did not take any preventive steps, did not demand stringent checks and balances, nor were they prepared for a calamity they knew could occur," he says.History has already shown the Trishuli River basin to be volatile, Thakkar says, pointing to how it had been hit by floods in the last two years. In September 2024, an unprecedented cloudburst over the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi river basins sparked flash floods in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading - settlements by the river that are also among the hardest hit from last week's floods.Then in July 2025, a glacial lake in Tibet's Gyirong county burst and swept down this very same stretch of river into Nepal, killing at least 11 people. That flood damaged critical infrastructure and halted trade along the busy Nepal-China corridor. The border crossing was shut for nearly six months and had only reopened on 1 January this year.Dhakal from the Nepal Electricity Authority admits that even if climate risk assessments were carried out correctly, "the designing of the plants may not have been done accordingly"."Clearly we will need to improve in the way we build and operate our hydropower plants," he adds.Private operators are already feeling the financial impact. Insurers have paid out around $40m for flood-related damage to more than 20 privately owned plants over the past three years, according to Uttam Bhlon Lama from the Independent Power Producers' Association of Nepal.He warns insurance premiums are rising significantly and making the cost of doing business "unfeasible".

schema.headline: Nepal bet nearly everything on hydropower - the floods show why that's a problem

title: Cave art discovery suggests first humans in Ireland came from Wales
description: Researchers believe the first known humans to set foot on Ireland thousands of years ago were most likely from Wales, following the "exciting" discove
body: Researchers believe the first known humans to set foot on Ireland thousands of years ago were most likely from Wales, following the "exciting" discovery of ancient cave art.During the most recent Ice Age, when much of the British Isles were beneath a vast continental glacier, the depleted sea levels opened a "lost land bridge" between modern-day Pembrokeshire and the south-east tip of Ireland, around Rosslare.According to rock expert Dr George Nash, from Liverpool University, the opportunities presented by this pathway would have been too good for hunter gatherers to ignore.Now, alongside an international team of experts, Nash has located eight cave sites in south-west Ireland featuring rock art dating back from at least 15,000 years ago, around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.Nash, who coordinated the Lost Land Bridge Project, said there would have been a forested and grassland plateau around 46 miles (76 km) coast-to-coast.With summertime temperatures typically -10°C to -20°C, Nash said the pathway would have supported wild horses, mammoth, bison, reindeer and other large herbivores, which fed off the hardy sedges, mosses and lichens growing through the fertile, but near-frozen soil.Nash said he had always believed - from what he had gleaned throughout his career about human movement during the period - that it was inconceivable that people would not have utilised the opportunity the pathway presented.This led him to assemble his multi-disciplinary team of experts from University College Dublin and the University of Adelaide, along with academics from Dubai, Wales and Portugal.

schema.headline: Cave art discovery suggests first humans in Ireland came from Wales

title: South Africa vs New Zealand: Siya Kolisi urges Boks to seize spirit of Soweto
description: Captain Siya Kolisi has called on the Springboks to summon inspiration from Soweto's pivotal part in South Africa's history as they take on New Zealan
body: Captain Siya Kolisi has called on the Springboks to summon inspiration from Soweto's pivotal part in South Africa's history as they take on New Zealand on the edge of the Johannesburg township on Saturday.The 94,736-capacity FNB Stadium staged the opening match of football's World Cup, the first and only time the tournament has been staged in Africa.However, Kolisi, South Africa's first black captain, also referenced 1976's Soweto Uprising - the student protests that were a turning point in the fight against apartheid, the state-backed racial segregation of South African society."So many things that happened in Soweto helped shape the South Africa we have today," said Kolisi."So many heroes have come from there, and a lot of the football history of this country is from Soweto, so we know how special that is."We're not going to act like it's not a special ground in a significant area. All of that gives us more to play for. We are also thankful for the people who came from there and fought for people like me and [assistant coach Mzwandile] Stick to be sitting here today."They fought for the freedom we have now and never got to experience it, and giving our best tomorrow is part of us saying thank you."The Soweto Uprising was a protest by school children and students against black schools being ordered to teach in English and Afrikaans, languages mainly used by the country's white population. Hundreds of protestors were killed by police as clashes continued and spread through Johannesburg.International condemnation of South Africa's government followed. Apartheid ended in 1994 with South Africa's first fully democratic elections.If both make it on to the field, they will become the second pair of brother-sister siblings to play for New Zealand on the same day, following Xavier and Annaleah Rush, who took on Australia at Sydney Football Stadium on 29 August 1998.Wallace and Amarante's father Semo Sititi, who played for Borders and Newcastle and captained Samoa, has travelled to Johannesburg for the match."Representing this country is a privilege but doing it alongside my brother is something special. I will always hold it in my heart," said Amarante., external "It's pretty surreal. I'm still buzzing out that I get to be here with my brother but it's really cool and I'm so grateful."South Africa: Kolbe; Arendse, Kriel, de Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Reinach; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi, PS du Toit, WieseReplacements: Fourie, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, Esterhuizen, Hanekom, Van den Berg, LibbokNew Zealand: McKenzie; Jordan, Tupaea, J Barrett, Carter; Love, Roigard; Bower, Aumua, Lomax, Vaa'I, Darry, Lakai, Jacobson, SaveaReplacements: Taukei'aho, Numia, Newell, Holland, Sititi, Preston, Lienert-Brown, Moorby

title: US Open 2026 results: Aryna Sabalenka's win over Kamilla Rakhimova interrupted by cannabis smell
description: Aryna Sabalenka briefly halted her US Open match against Kamilla Rakhimova because of a strong smell of cannabis before cruising into the fourth round
body: Aryna Sabalenka briefly halted her US Open match against Kamilla Rakhimova because of a strong smell of cannabis before cruising into the fourth round in New York.Top seed Sabalenka raised the issue after going 3-0 up in the first set against Uzbekistan's Rakhimova, telling umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore that "someone is smoking weed".The Belarusian asked the umpire to intervene "because it's so strong".Asderaki-Moore spoke to an official on her radio and made a smoking gesture to someone behind her, before play continued.Two-time defending champion Sabalenka went on to secure a confident 6-3 6-4 victory on Louis Armstrong Stadium as she chases a fifth Grand Slam singles title.Sabalenka said afterwards she was not sure where the smell of cannabis was coming from but asked fans to be more mindful.Smoking is not permitted on site at Flushing Meadows but the smell of cannabis sometimes wafts on to court from the nearby Corona Park.It is legal to smoke it in New York for adults aged 21 and over."It's a bit tricky to handle that smell while you're trying to compete at your best," Sabalenka said."I don't know if it was coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium. "I just hope they're going to be a bit more aware of that stuff."Sabalenka is not the first player at this year's US Open to complain about the smell of cannabis at Flushing Meadows.Britain's Katie Boulter previously said it was distracting, while Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones also noticed the smell.In past years players including Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev have also complained.American third seed Jessica Pegula kept her bid for a first Grand Slam title alive by coming from a set down to beat Leylah Fernandez.Pegula, who lost the final at Flushing Meadows two years ago to Sabalenka, came through 1-6 6-4 6-3 against the Canadian 31st seed.Fernandez showed glimpses of the form that took her to the 2021 US Open final, where she lost to Emma Raducanu, as she raced through the first set in under 30 minutes.But Pegula played with more patience to secure the decisive break at the end of the second set - albeit with some help from a net cord.She saved two break points at the start of the deciding set, before breaking in the next game and going on to see out victory with a backhand volley."I wasn't moving my feet up to the ball, and I was a little lazy to start off," Pegula, 32, said."I was going to have to dig deep. I'm glad I was able to find somewhere there in the second set to turn it around."Pegula will play Romanian 16th seed Sorana Cirstea in the fourth round after she beat Italian 19th seed Jasmine Paolini 6-3 6-3.Later, Czech seventh seed Muchova lost 6-3 7-5 to American 26th seed Navarro.Muchova had been competing in her first tournament since undergoing minor surgery after reaching July's Wimbledon final.Navarro will play Ukrainian ninth seed Elina Svitolina or Russian 21st seed Anna Kalinskaya in the fourth round.Ukrainian 11th seed Marta Kostyuk is also safely though to the last-16 after beating Ekaterina Alexandrova 6-3 6-2 and will face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova next.In the women's doubles, Britons Harriet Dart and Maia Lumsden ousted Croatia's Petra Marcinko and Ukraine's Oleksandra Oliynykova 7-5 6-3 to reach the second round.

title: Retatutride: How the hunger for a new weight loss drug is feeding an industry of fakes
description: Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.But
body: Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.But new weight-loss drug retatrutide has become a headache not only for Eli Lilly, the pharmaceutical company behind it, but for regulators in the UK and around the world.The jab has not yet been approved for human use by any regulatory body.But illicit, counterfeit dupes of retatrutide are currently flooding the black market.Experts have told the BBC this is one of the first times they have seen copycat versions of an experimental drug, still in the throes of being tested, become so widely available.Vials purporting to be "reta" as it's become known, are being sold in the UK in gyms, nail and beauty salons, hairdressers, on social media and even by flower sellers on the street."The world has gone mad," pharmacist and director of 24 HR Pharmacy, Sehar Shahid says. "People are effectively injecting an illegal drug and thinking it's safe."It's become so normalised people openly talk about their dealers, where's best to get it from and post all over social media."One quick flick through my socials and I can order a batch of a drug billed as retatrutide in minutes - although I would have no proof what it's actually made of, what its effects would be and where it's come from.Keen users are posting before and after "reta" pics on their TikTok feeds, describing how it has silenced food noise, helped them shed pounds and lose inches, with some saying it's completely transformed their lives.The problem? Despite positive results in its most recent clinical trials, real retatrutide is still being tested for its safety and efficacy. Only 50% of drugs in this Phase III stage of testing in the US are eventually approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), so there is no guarantee retatrutide will ever hit the market. The high rate of failure is primarily down to drugs not working as well in large, diverse human populations as they do in smaller early tests, or because they reveal unexpected safety hazards.And the current, fake versions available may not resemble what's being developed in the safe confines of the laboratory.Eli Lilly's website carries a strong warning "no one should take anything claiming to be retatrutide outside of a Lilly-sponsored clinical trial". "Illicit retatrutide products may contain unknown ingredients, harmful contaminants and impurities. These products may also have too much or too little active ingredient, or the wrong ingredient entirely".Despite this, it seems there are plenty of people willing to take that gamble."Young fit patients are coming into hospital with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, in some cases kidney failure," says endocrinologist, Prof Donal O'Shea.He says some personal trainers are not only supplying their clients with the drug, they are also injecting them with it."The patients have no idea how much they have been taking, or even what they've been injected with."Tom Davies says he nearly ended up in hospital after accidentally overdosing on a fake version of retatrutide. He ordered it from a Chinese supplier after friends at his gym recommended it."It was horrendous," says the 20-year-old from Brighton. "My body felt so under pressure, I was so bloated, it was like someone had dropped a 20kg weight on my stomach."For 72 hours I had really bad diarrhoea and nausea. I thought, if this continues I'm going to end up in A&E."Tom later realised he had given himself eight times the recommended dose. Depending on what is ordered, copycat retatrutide can arrive needing to be mixed with sterile, bacteriostatic water which requires various calculations.Dr Nas Khattak, a research doctor based in Chester, has been screening patients for one of Eli Lilly's Phase III clinical trials. He says those sourcing fake versions are in effect behaving as lab rats without any medical oversight."If users who buy it online become their own doctor, they're taking a huge risk," he warns.He says trial participants need to meet strict criteria before they are given the green light to start taking the real drug or a placebo."We request their GP record, we make sure that they're emotionally well. They'll have suicide, self-harm, mental health assessments - and this is all done by doctors."Then we come back and have a look at the blood tests, have a look at everything, and then we think whether they're suitable or not."Tom decided to do more research into dosing and, despite the nasty side effects he'd previously experienced, decided to give his fake version of retatrutide another go. After nine months of taking it in cycles, he says his cravings for sugar and junk food have gone.Pharmacist Shahid warns that just because a fake version of reta works for one person, does not mean it will "work for the next".The obesity drugs currently on the market - the likes of semaglutide (marketed as Ozempic and Wegovy), and tirzepatide (marketed as Mounjaro) - target just one or two hormone receptors. But, if approved, retatrutide will become the first weight loss medication in the world to act on three, giving it the nickname the "triple G".The three hormones it mimics are: GLP-1 - this slows down stomach emptying, signals fullness to the brain to reduce appetite and helps control blood sugar levelsGIP - this enhances insulin secretion and improves insulin sensitivity, and works alongside GLP-1 to help the body process nutrients and reduces hungerGlucagon - this is the hormone that's novel to retatrutide. It increases resting energy expenditure so the body burns more calories, promotes liver fat breakdown and supports weight loss.Lisa King has been taking a fake version of retatrutide since July and at one stage, while she was also going to the gym and eating healthily, she was losing 3kg (6lb) a week.It's also, she believes, helping her manage some of the symptoms of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). GLP-1s help regulate blood sugar, and some studies suggest these weight-loss drugs can help with some of the problems caused by PMOS, which can bring about extreme tiredness, kidney problems and high blood pressure."I'm not sure if it's due to reta," Lisa says, "but my sugar cravings have gone down, my periods have regulated and I've got a lot more energy."But retatrutide is still in trials. Does this bother her?"No," she says, "not at all. There are many things that have not been approved."If I start to experience any negative side effects I'll just come straight off it."Other users taking counterfeit versions of retatrutide have reported a range of issues including brain fog, nausea, diarrhoea, a loss of libido and no longer being able to feel any happiness or joy.Doctors are becoming increasingly worried about the side effects they are seeing amongst users of these counterfeit weight-loss drugs.Dr Sahira Dar, a GP and chair of the British Islamic Medical Association, says healthcare professionals should ask about black market products "without judgement", so patients feel able to "disclose what they have taken".Eli Lilly has been developing retatrutide for nearly 10 years. It is now fighting to protect its product and curb the illegal sales which are taking place across the world.It's taking action against peptide companies, influencers, compound pharmacies which manufacture the fake medication, and wellness clinics. It has reported more than 14,000 websites, advertisements and social media posts it says are illegally marketing the medication.Eli Lilly says it "continues to work with law enforcement and regulatory authorities to combat black market drugs".A spokesperson told the BBC: "Any retatrutide available online is unapproved, unverified and simply not worth the risk."The UK's Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has carried out raids and made several seizures of "products claiming to contain retatrutide" over the past year.It says there are a number of different routes these products enter the UK and it is working to "disrupt illegal importation and distribution".But the sales continue.Prof O'Shea says while we need to "shine a light on the dangers of such black market drugs", we should not "trash this family of medications"."GLP-1s are a major advance in managing obesity, a major advance in our insight into how the brain regulates cravings and appetite."That," he says, "is huge".For now, there is still a long way to go before retatrutide gets approval anywhere.Eli Lilly plans to submit its application for US FDA approval early next year. It can take up to a year to carry out a review, so retatrutide would not be legally available in the US until the end of 2027 at the earliest.In the UK, depending on the approval of the MHRA, it could be on the market by 2028.

schema.headline: Retatutride: How the hunger for a new weight loss drug is feeding an industry of fakes

title: Virgin's Richard Branson: Flight price rises due to 'foolish leaders' starting wars
description: Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Isra
body: Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.Middle East tensions have choked the production and transportation of millions of barrels of oil, causing a surge in the price of car and jet fuels, which are made from oil.In May, Virgin Atlantic added a fuel surcharge to ticket prices in response.US President Donald Trump has repeatedly defended the conflict as necessary for peace and security long-term.However, Sir Richard said there was "no need" for the war. "The Iran conflict was completely unnecessary. There was a nuclear agreement between Iran and the rest of the world that had been negotiated by President Obama and a lot of European people."It was working, so there was no need to rip it up... And this war has just resulted in much higher oil prices all over the world. And inflation has been one of the consequences."The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.The European benchmark jet fuel price had been hovering around $800 (£590) a tonne but spiked following the outbreak of the Iran war, reaching a peak of over $1,800 in April. It has since dropped to around $1,450. Virgin Atlantic's chief executive, Corneel Koster, told the BBC that for "this level of fuel price" fuel surcharges were "absolutely required", adding that it's "hard to be optimistic at this moment about the situation in the Middle East".The surcharge Virgin introduced added £50 to an economy class fare, £180 to premium and £360 to business class.

schema.headline: Virgin's Richard Branson: Flight price rises due to 'foolish leaders' starting wars

title: Cambridge launches review into support for Jason Arday before death
description: The University of Cambridge has launched an independent review into its "decision-making and actions" in the period leading up to former professor Jas
body: The University of Cambridge has launched an independent review into its "decision-making and actions" in the period leading up to former professor Jason Arday's death.The review will examine the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.Arday, 41, was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, the week after resigning from his position as professor of sociology of education amid intense scrutiny over allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims.Announcing the review on Friday, Vice-Chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice said the time since his death had been a "period of profound sadness and reflection for the university"."We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus, but given the devastating outcome, we are still asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more," she said."This review will help us answer that question."In a post on social media, the University of Cambridge said: "University Council took the necessary steps to launch an independent review into the university's decision-making and actions, with a focus on identifying shortcomings and areas for improvement."The first part of the review will look at the "support, interventions and protections" available to Arday in the period before his death.Those findings will be reported within three months, allowing recommendations for "urgent action" to be considered and implemented "without delay".It will be led by Nazir Afzal, chancellor of the University of Manchester and former chief crown prosecutor for the North West of England. Afzal said in a statement that "it is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity", adding "we must be willing to ask difficult questions".The second part of the review will examine the wider circumstances of Arday's time at Cambridge, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, mentoring and support arrangements.It will also look at the university's response to allegations of research misconduct and the support available to academics facing "extraordinary public and media scrutiny".An independent external chair will be appointed to lead the second part of the review, with an expert panel "including individuals with lived experience" advising it.It is expected to conclude within six months of the panel being established.In a video message, Prentice said: "I am conscious that Professor Arday's death has deeply affected black staff and students, as well as our neurodiverse community."There has also been an unacceptable rise in racist, hateful, and abusive attacks on our staff and students in online forums and on social media."In 2023, the sociologist, then 37, became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge.Arday had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work. Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. He said similar scrutiny would find comparable errors in the work of other academics.The allegations emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.Arday said the criticism had gone "far beyond scholarly disagreement".Resigning from his post in August, he added: "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and those I love."Following his death, his family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."A vigil held in Trafalgar Square was attended by thousands, according to its organisers.There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage of Arday before his death.

schema.headline: Cambridge launches review into support for Jason Arday before death

title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
description: Image source, Tomas Cuesta/Getty ImagesImage caption, Argentine President Javier Milei enjoys a warm relationship with President TrumpByWill GrantBBC'
body: Image source, Tomas Cuesta/Getty ImagesImage caption, Argentine President Javier Milei enjoys a warm relationship with President TrumpByWill GrantBBC's Mexico, Central America and Cuba correspondentThe tone over the Falkland Islands dispute has been sharpening in Argentina from well before President Javier Milei's late-night national address on sanctions earlier this week.It's tempting to see a visual representation of the tension in the jubilant Argentine players celebrating their hard-fought win over England at the Fifa World Cup this summer holding a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentine - in front of their deliriously happy fans. However, the ill-feeling has been fomenting for much longer.President Milei began his Thursday address with a brief history of the Falklands, very much from the Argentine perspective. He repeated the refrain at the heart of their position: the islands "rightfully belong" to Argentina. The British had invaded and colonially occupied the islands in 1833, he said, violently wrestling the territory from Argentina's hands.The UK Government would say he conveniently overlooked a few details: the islands – over which the European powers had interchanged control throughout the 17th and 18th centuries – were uninhabited at the time the British reoccupied the land. The Argentine settlement had been forced out two years earlier, not by the British but by the Americans. A warship, the USS Lexington, destroyed a fort established there in December 1831 amid a dispute over local fishing and sealing rights.Still, if the Americans had a hand in forcing the Argentines out two centuries ago, they may now play a central role in strengthening the Argentine claim. President Milei certainly thinks so."Winds of change" were blowing, he assured the Argentine people, after President Trump said he was "re-evaluating" the US position on the Falklands. Image source, Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesImage caption, The US recognises Britain's rule over the Falklands - but Trump has suggested he is "re-evaluating" the US positionThat position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982  – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict.For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran."You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific.Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his former vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing.Image source, REUTERS/Amanda PerobelliImage caption, Fifa fined the Argentine Football Association after players held up a banner claiming the Falklands, breaching rules against political messagingDomestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake exploration work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally. The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".

schema.headline: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder

title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says
description: Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a go
body: Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country."It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously."If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't."So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply. It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.Defra said the report showed food supply risks were becoming more complex and the government was working with farmers and industry to strengthen the UK's resilience."While our food businesses and supermarkets have continued to feed the nation through significant disruption, we will carefully consider the report's findings and recommendations as part of our ongoing work to build a more resilient, productive and sustainable food system," a spokesperson said.In July, the government announced plans to set out the "small but important steps" households can take to prepare for food and water shortages in the event of extreme weather or cyber-attacks. These will form a strategy to be unveiled by the end of 2026 aimed at bringing the UK closer into line with European countries in terms of emergency preparedness. Phil Pluck, chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, the body which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, said Britain was "pretty close to crisis".He told the BBC's Wake Up to Money programme that the country was being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".He added that El Niño, as well as global shipping disruption and the threat of pandemics, mean you cannot "just rely on the private sector coming through every single time".Asked whether people should be stocking up in case of disruptions, Pluck added: "Yes, we should."There should be some sensible stocking in each household. And the government in the autumn will be telling all of us to do that."

schema.headline: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says
